messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is an eighteen-year-old African American man who joined the police force only months ago, driven in part by a conviction — formed early and held tightly — that someone should be able to stop violence before it destroys a family. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 77, reporting a constellation of symptoms severe enough that his supervising sergeant recently placed him on restricted duty after Kofi froze during a domestic disturbance call. That incident, and the shame that followed, is what finally brought him through the door of the department's counselling service.

The trauma Kofi carries is not a single night but a pattern that repeated across most of his childhood: his father's rages, the sound of furniture overturned, his mother's muffled crying through a closed door, and on the worst occasions, the specific, terrible stillness that fell over the apartment just before the violence escalated. He was rarely the direct target, but he was always present — small, motionless in a corner, his body braced. He remembers one night with particular acuity: he was perhaps nine years old, standing in the kitchen doorway, watching his father lift a glass bottle from the counter. The image lives in him as a sequence of frozen frames — his father's hand around the neck of the bottle, his mother's face turning, the particular quality of silence in the room. Each moment is a photograph rather than a film, and they arrive without warning.

Since beginning his patrol duties, Kofi has found that the job delivers his triggers with near-daily regularity. When he responds to calls in unfamiliar neighbourhoods, the moment he steps out of the cruiser and scans the environment, his eyes move involuntarily to potential weapons — a loose brick, a kitchen knife visible through a window, a man holding a belt — before he has consciously registered anything else. That hypervigilance, already present, sharpens further when he encounters unusual silence on a scene; the absence of noise carries for him the exact atmospheric charge of that kitchen doorway, and the stillness alone is enough to pull the frozen images forward into full awareness. When those memories surface on the job — the bottle, the braced body, the grief that accompanies every recollection of his mother's face — his threat monitoring intensifies in response, his body reading the past as present danger, and he begins scanning even more compulsively for anything that might function as a weapon. The loop is not subtle. A colleague touched his shoulder unexpectedly last month while he was filling out a report, and Kofi's body went rigid in the posture of that nine-year-old in the doorway — his shoulders drawn in, his chin dropping — before he could locate himself in the present. The physical reenactment was visible enough that the colleague asked if he was all right.

What frightens Kofi most, beyond the memories themselves, is what he has concluded about their meaning. He has come to believe that he cannot rely on himself — that a man who freezes at a shoulder touch has no business carrying a badge — and this conviction that he is fundamentally unreliable has begun to colour how he reads the world around him. Because he cannot trust his own capacity to protect himself or others, every unfamiliar environment feels unassessable, and he avoids them when off duty, keeping to the same three or four blocks near his apartment. He is also increasingly certain that his reactions — the bodily reenactments, the intrusive grief, the way silence makes his pulse climb — mean that something in him has broken in a way that ordinary people do not break. The fear that he is going crazy is not a passing thought; it is a conclusion he returns to daily. These appraisals of helplessness and self-distrust feed directly into his threat monitoring: if he cannot rely on himself to judge danger accurately, then everything must be pre-emptively treated as dangerous, and so his vigilance never fully disengages. That sustained state of threat, in turn, makes him more sensitive to the very triggers — sudden touch, suspicious behaviour, unnatural quiet — that collapse the distance between now and then.

Kofi comes to therapy hoping, cautiously, that someone can tell him he is not losing his mind. What he is most afraid of is that they cannot.
